content.text:
The file is updated. It was a 41-byte empty root element, so there was no drawing to improve. I made it a proper SVG skeleton and left the content for you to define.

The original had nothing but `<svg xmlns=...>`: no size, no coordinate system, no accessible name, and no trailing newline. Browsers render such a file at a default 300 by 150 box and screen readers have nothing to announce.

The file now reads:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100">
  <title>Placeholder</title>
</svg>
```

What changed and why:

- **XML declaration** with an explicit encoding, so desktop tools and older converters read the standalone file correctly.
- **Intrinsic size and viewBox** give the image a defined 100 by 100 coordinate system and a predictable size when embedded or opened directly.
- **A title element** gives assistive technology an accessible name.
- **Trailing newline** so the file follows text-file convention and diffs cleanly.

Two things to flag. First, the sandbox denied every shell command after the initial listing, including xmllint and a tool check, so I could not run external validation or a render. The file is four simple, properly closed elements, and I verified it by inspection. Second, the canvas size and the title text are my assumptions. The image still renders as a blank square because nothing in the original said what it should show. If you tell me what it should depict, for example the digit zero suggested by the filename, I'll draw it into this skeleton and update the title.
